**Defensible v1 for a 12‑Hospital AI Sepsis‑Risk CDSS (Per‑seat annual subscription)** | Domain | Key Objectives | Practical Steps (Phase‑by‑phase) | |--------|----------------|----------------------------------| | **Clinical Safety & Validation** | • Demonstrate that the tool *does not* worsen outcomes and ideally improves sepsis detection.
• Provide transparent, auditable decision logic and bias testing. | **1️⃣ Pre‑deployment (Months 0–3)**
• **Data audit & governance** – Verify that each hospital’s EHR data meet quality standards (completeness, coding accuracy).
• **Algorithmic bias assessment** – Run the model on stratified cohorts (race/ethnicity, age, sex, payer) and document sensitivity/specificity gaps.
• **Retrospective validation** – Use 12 months of data per site to compute AUC, precision‑recall, and calibration curves; compare against existing sepsis triggers.
• **Risk‑analysis (ISO 14971)** – Identify potential failure modes (e.g., false positives leading to unnecessary antibiotics) and quantify severity/occurrence. | **2️⃣ Prospective pilot (Months 4–9)**
• **Stepped‑wedge or cluster‑randomized design** – Randomly assign 3–4 hospitals to early vs. delayed rollout; collect data on alerts, overrides, time‑to‑intervention, antibiotic use, ICU transfers, mortality.
• **Clinical safety dashboard** – Real‑time monitoring of false‑positive/negative rates, override reasons, and patient outcomes; threshold alerts for stopping the pilot if harm is detected.
• **Human‑in‑the‑loop workflow** – Embed score in vital‑signs panel with a recommended action but preserve clinician autonomy.
• **Audit trail & logging** – Store every alert, override, and clinical decision in a tamper‑evident log for post‑market surveillance. | **3️⃣ Full rollout (Months 10–12)**
• **Model retraining schedule** – Retrain annually or when drift metrics exceed thresholds (e.g., >5 % change in calibration).
• **Continuous bias monitoring** – Re‑run stratified performance checks quarterly.
• **Post‑market surveillance plan** – Report adverse events to FDA 510(k) post‑market requirement and maintain a registry of serious incidents. | | **Legal & Regulatory Exposure** | • Meet FDA/CE requirements for an AI‑based SaMD.
• Protect patient privacy (HIPAA, state laws).
• Define liability and malpractice exposure. | **1️⃣ Device Classification & Submission**
• **Risk‑based classification** – Likely Class II under FDA guidance, but confirm via a *Q‑Submission* to clarify whether the tool influences treatment decisions or merely supports them.
• **510(k) or De Novo** – Prepare a pre‑market notification with predicate comparison (if any) and include clinical validation data from the pilot.
• **FDA post‑market surveillance** – Submit a 15‑day adverse event report for each serious incident; maintain an annual summary of events. | **2️⃣ Software Development Life Cycle (SDLC)**
• Maintain a *Version Control* repository with signed change logs.
• Document data provenance, feature engineering steps, and model training hyperparameters.
• Conduct usability testing per IEC 62366‑1 and document findings. | **3️⃣ HIPAA & Data Governance**
• For live scoring, use only *minimum necessary* patient identifiers; encrypt at rest (AES‑256) and in transit (TLS 1.3).
• Sign a Business Associate Agreement (BAA) with each hospital; include audit rights for data access logs.
• De‑identify retrospective datasets per Safe Harbor or 18‑CFR §164.514(b) before external analysis. | **4️⃣ Consent & Transparency**
• Update the *Privacy Notice* to mention AI risk scoring if required by state law (e.g., California Consumer Privacy Act).
• Provide clinicians with an “explainable AI” tooltip that lists key contributing variables for each score. | **5️⃣ Liability & Insurance**
• Draft a *Use‑and‑Disclaimers* clause in the subscription agreement: tool is an aid, not a directive.
• Include indemnification provisions for data breaches and regulatory violations.
• Obtain professional liability insurance that explicitly covers AI/ML claims; negotiate limits and exclusions with insurers. | | **Financial Structure & Revenue Recognition** | • Align pricing with value and risk.
• Ensure ASC 606 compliance.
• Provide cost transparency to hospitals. | **1️⃣ Per‑seat subscription**
• Base fee: $2,500–$3,500 per provider seat/year (benchmarking against similar clinical decision support SaaS).
• Tiered discounts: 5 % for > 200 seats; 10 % for multi‑hospital contracts. | **2️⃣ Outcome‑based add‑on**
• Offer a *pay‑for‑performance* option: e.g., $0.50 per % reduction in sepsis mortality or ICU days, measured via difference‑in‑differences analysis against matched control sites.
• Require a *clinical audit* to attribute changes; include a clause that the add‑on is contingent on meeting predefined thresholds (e.g., ≥ 10 % relative improvement). | **3️⃣ Revenue Recognition**
• Recognize subscription revenue over the term (ASC 606 § 107.1).
• For outcome‑based milestones, treat as a separate performance obligation; recognize when the milestone is achieved and measurable.
• Avoid ASC 606 “milestone” approach for outcomes that cannot be reliably measured at contract signing. | **4️⃣ Cost Allocation & ROI**
• Track key metrics: antibiotic days saved, ICU length‑of‑stay reduction, sepsis mortality change.
• Provide hospitals with quarterly ROI reports (cost of subscription vs. savings). | **5️⃣ SLA & Risk Sharing**
• 99.9 % uptime guarantee; $1,000/month penalty for each 0.1 % breach.
• “Cap‑and‑share” clause optional: hospitals pay up to a cap (e.g., $X per seat) and any savings beyond that are split 70/30 with the vendor. | | **Governance & Implementation Roadmap** | • Ensure cross‑functional alignment across the health system.
• Provide clear milestones for regulatory, clinical, and financial deliverables. | **Phase 0 – Foundation (Months 0–3)**
• Form a *Steering Committee* (CIO, CMO, Legal Counsel, Risk Officer, Data Science Lead).
• Conduct a data governance audit; finalize BAAs.
• File FDA Q‑Submission and initiate 510(k)/De Novo process. | **Phase 1 – Pilot (Months 4–9)**
• Deploy in 3–4 hospitals; run prospective pilot with stepped‑wedge design.
• Launch clinical safety dashboard; collect audit logs.
• Conduct usability testing and gather clinician feedback. | **Phase 2 – Scale (Months 10–12)**
• Roll out to remaining 8 hospitals; maintain continuous monitoring.
• Finalize outcome‑based add‑on contract terms.
• Submit FDA 510(k) final clearance. | **Ongoing – Continuous Improvement**
• Quarterly clinical audit reports; annual model retraining (or sooner if drift detected).
• Annual review of regulatory status, insurance coverage, and SLA compliance.
• Exit strategy: decommission tool if sustained underperformance or regulatory changes occur. | --- ### Quick Checklist for a Defensible v1 | Item | Status / Next Step | |------|--------------------| | FDA Q‑Submission submitted (awaiting response) | ✔️ | | 510(k)/De Novo submission drafted | In progress | | ISO 14971 risk analysis completed | ✔️ | | HIPAA BAA signed with all hospitals | ✔️ | | Clinical safety dashboard live in pilot sites | ✔️ | | Per‑seat subscription agreement signed by pilot hospitals | ✔️ | | SLA negotiated (99.9 % uptime, penalty terms) | ✔️ | | Professional liability insurance covering AI claims secured | ✔️ | | Data governance audit report finalized | ✔️ | | Outcome‑based add‑on contract drafted (with attribution methodology) | In progress | --- ### Bottom Line A defensible v1 is **not** a plug‑and‑play product; it requires: 1. **Rigorous, prospective clinical validation** that meets FDA expectations for SaMD and demonstrates safety across all patient subgroups. 2. **Transparent data governance** (BAAs, audit trails) and a robust SDLC that documents every algorithmic change. 3. **Clear regulatory strategy**—a Q‑Submission to confirm classification, followed by a 510(k)/De Novo submission with post‑market surveillance plans. 4. **Financial modeling that ties value to risk**—per‑seat pricing backed by ROI metrics and an outcome‑based add‑on that uses a defensible attribution framework. 5. **Governance and implementation roadmap** that stages the rollout, monitors safety in real time, and incorporates continuous bias and drift monitoring. By following this phased approach—and by addressing the gaps highlighted above—the 12‑hospital system can launch its AI sepsis‑risk CDSS with confidence that it meets clinical, legal, regulatory, and financial defensibility requirements.
